title: Big Elections Always Wash Some Oddballs Into Office. Meet the Wave Weirdos of 2026.

 Big Elections Always Wash Some Oddballs Into Office. Meet the Wave Weirdos of 2026.
 A felon, a college student, and a dairy farmer walk into a state house …
 By
 Ian Prasad Philbrick

 This story is adapted from the Slatest newsletter. You can sign up here to get it in your inbox every day. 
 My first grown-up journalism job coincided with the 2018 midterms, a wave election powered by a backlash to Donald Trump (sound familiar?). At one point, in my naivete, I said something about the many unorthodox Democratic candidates that wave washed into office: democratic socialists, a former mixed martial artist, an openly bisexual Arizona senator, and more. To which an esteemed colleague responded with something like: Yeah, waves always elect some weirdos .
 I don’t believe he meant it as an insult; many surprise 2018 winners are still in office. But the line captures a quirky truth about American politics: Wave elections can give young, controversial, or otherwise long-shot candidates the boost they need to win, and the blue tsunami of 2026 was no exception. Let’s survey some of the stranger Democratic contenders who found themselves unexpectedly swept to victory this month:
 • 
 Video from Slate 
 Nathan Miller: A long-haired, overalls-wearing dairy farmer, Miller threw his knit hat in the ring for county assessor largely to protest the fact that Republicans in his deep-red Arkansas county often ran unopposed. Miller was reportedly milking a cow in his barn when he learned he was on track to win.
 Sebastian Matta: A 19-year-old philosophy major at Arizona State University will be Maricopa County’s next Superior Court clerk, managing court records, marriage licenses, and other documents for the country’s fourth-most-populous county. Matta won the Democratic primary uncontested, describing himself as a “sacrificial-lamb” candidate . 
 Ericka Lomick: She suspended her campaign for a heavily Republican Texas Statehouse seat in September after revelations that she’d been convicted of mortgage and bank fraud. But Lomick won anyway, and now her GOP opponent is trying to block her from taking office .
 Daniel Darris-O’Connor: Another 19-year-old college student beat a 16-year GOP incumbent in the Massachusetts Statehouse —despite occasionally getting mistaken for an intern while campaigning. According to CBS News, “Darris-O’Connor’s interest in politics began during the COVID-19 pandemic, when he was a seventh grader.” Now I feel old! 
 Eric Armstrong: Another Democrat who ended his campaign before Election Day, in this case citing “personal health issues,” Armstrong won an Iowa Statehouse seat after his name stayed on the ballot. Despite his health issues, he plans to take office in January .
 Hipolito Cerros: A 28-year-old former small-town mayor ousted the top state Assembly Republican in a deep-red California district. Per Politico , Cerros raised no money and had zero campaign staff.
 Calling these long-shot winners weird is no insult: They’re interesting because they defied the normal rules of politics. Republicans have sometimes gotten similar breaks. In 2021, a furniture truck driver named Ed Durr unexpectedly toppled New Jersey’s longtime Democratic Senate president after spending just $2,300 on the race.
 But wave winners’ stories don’t always end happily. Durr handily lost reelection the next cycle. Kyrsten Sinema, who in 2018 became the first Democrat to win an Arizona U.S. Senate seat in decades, later became a thorn in her party’s side, quit the Senate, and this year supported a (losing) GOP House candidate . So as this year’s blue tsunami recedes, we’ll have to wait for future elections to separate the skilled surfers from the flukes.
 Tolga Akdoğan

 It’s finally Friday. And whether you’re feeling energized for the weekend or washed out after a long week, my colleagues have some great reads to wrap up your day: 
 Get some special holiday advice from Michelle Obama: Your aunt has opinions about the stuffing, your in-laws aren’t speaking, and your seating chart is starting to look like a diplomatic crisis. Luckily, we have a Guest Prudence who has survived a state dinner or two. Michelle Obama shares the clever shortcut she used to dodge Thanksgiving cooking duty, the one appliance she says every host needs, and her secret weapon for unexpected holiday guests .

 Stay safe on the road: As Americans live longer, car crashes involving elderly drivers are on the rise—and we all need to understand what’s coming. David Howard lays out the risks we face and provides ample fodder if you need to talk with an aging parent or relative about when to give up the car keys .
 Advertisement 
 Say goodbye to Fiona the Hippo: Fiona, a Nile hippo at the Cincinnati Zoo who rose to internet fame after being born prematurely, was beloved for her resilience and sassy personality. Sadly, Fiona died this week after ingesting a hat that blew into her enclosure. ICYMI host Kate Lindsay pays tribute to this majestic animal, gone too soon .
 Watch a masterful new crime drama: Paper Tiger , a new mob epic set in 1980s New York, is an exquisitely crafted movie starring Scarlett Johansson, Adam Driver, and Miles Teller. Slate film critic Dana Stevens describes it as “a combination Ancient Greek tragedy and neo-noir Hollywood gangster saga .”
 And with that, I’m out! Enjoy the weekend, and see you back here on Monday.
